source_text: XIII. Interim ceteri ducebantur ad victimae locum. concursus fit undique gentilium et omnium fratrum, qui quamvis obsequentes aliis et ceteris dei testibus pro religione et fide, quam Cypriano docente didicerant, tunc tamen officio pleniore et copia maiore convenerant. erat illic videre martyres Christi felicitatem gloriae suae vultus hilaritate testantes, ita ut possent ceteros provocare ad propriae virtutis exempla, etiamsi tacerent. sed nec sermonis largitas defuit. nam cohortatibus suis singuli plebem corroboraverunt. et Lucium quidem praeter ingenitam lenitatem et probam ac modestam verecundiam infirmitas etiam gravis et labor carceris fregerat, ac propterea cum comitibus paucioribus solus ante praecessit, ne multitudinis nimiae pressura defusioni sanguinis invideret. qui tamen et ipse non tacuit, sed comites suos quomodo potuit instruxit. cui cum dicerent fratres: Memento nostri, Vos, inquit, mei mementote. quanta martyris humilitas, de gloria sua nec sub ipsa passione praesumere! Iulianus quoque et Victoricus insinuata diu fratribus pace et commendatis omnibus clericis, maxime eis qui famem carceris visitaverant, ad passionis locum cum gaudio et sine pavore venerant.
orientation: The editor narrates the condemned confessors being led out to execution after Flavian was taken back into custody.
pass_a_gloss: Meanwhile the rest were being led to the place of the sacrifice. A gathering took place from everywhere of pagans and of all the brothers, who although devoted to others and to the other witnesses of God on account of religion and faith, which they had learned with Cyprian teaching, then nevertheless had come together with fuller duty and with greater number. It was there to see the witnesses of Christ testifying to the blessedness of their own glory by cheerfulness of face, so that they were able to call forth the rest to examples of their own courage, even if they kept silent. But neither was abundance of speech lacking. For by their exhortations each strengthened the people. And as for Lucius, besides inborn gentleness and upright and modest shame, severe weakness also and the toil of prison had broken him, and for this reason with fewer companions he alone went ahead before, in order that the hardship of too great a crowd not begrudge the pouring out of blood. Yet he himself did not keep silent either, but instructed his companions as he was able. When the brothers were saying to him, Remember us, he said, You remember me. How great the humility of the witness, to presume nothing concerning his own glory not even under the suffering itself! Julian also and Victoricus, with peace long urged upon the brothers and all the clergy commended, especially those who had visited the hunger of the prison, had come to the place of suffering with joy and without fear.

pass_b_english: Meanwhile the rest were led to the place of the sacrifice. People streamed together from every side, outsiders as well as all the brothers. Although they were already devoted to the other witnesses of God, for the sake of the religion and faith they had learned when Cyprian taught them, they now gathered with fuller service and in greater numbers. There you could see the martyrs of Christ, the brightness of their faces testifying to the joy of their glory. Even if they had said nothing, they could have called the rest to follow their courage. But words were not lacking either, for each of them strengthened the people with his urging. Lucius, besides his inborn gentleness and his upright and modest reserve, had also been broken by serious illness and the hardship of prison. So he went ahead alone with fewer companions, lest the crush of too great a crowd hinder the shedding of blood. Yet he too did not keep silent, but taught his companions as best he could. When the brothers said to him, "Remember us," Lucius says, "You remember me." What humility in a martyr, to claim nothing for his own glory even in the very moment of suffering! Julian and Victoricus also, after long urging peace upon the brothers and commending all the clergy, especially those who had visited them in the hunger of prison, came to the place of suffering with joy and without fear.

problems.quote: lest the hardship of too great a multitude begrudge the shedding of blood
problems.source_quote: ne multitudinis nimiae pressura defusioni sanguinis invideret
problems.why: pressura here is physical crowd-crush, not hardship; invidere means hinder/deprive, not begrudge
problems.fix: lest the crush of too great a crowd interfere with the shedding of his blood
problems.ruling: "pressura" in "multitudinis nimiae pressura" is the crush of the crowd, not "hardship". The English loses the point that the crowd's press might obstruct the execution.

edits.old: lest the hardship of too great a multitude begrudge the shedding of blood
edits.new: lest the crush of too great a crowd hinder the shedding of blood

fixed: Fixed pressura/invidere: source has multitudinis nimiae pressura = physical crush/pressure of the crowd, not hardship, and invideret defusioni sanguinis = hinder the shedding, not begrudge.
